author: Kevin Kinder
title: WVU's win over Marshall shouldn't be overlooked ahead of its road trip to Kansas | Jackson Star and Herald - Ripley and Ravenswood | wvnews.com
text:
CHARLESTON, W.Va. -- Those who didn't cover in person, or pay much attention to, West Virginia's 7-2 win over Marshall at decrepit GoMart Ballpark in Charleston on Tuesday evening missed several items of importance.
The first thing was the result of the game itself, which provided another series sweep for the Mountaineers, albeit with the caveat that the contests ranged over the period of 43 days. Even though some of these same pundits say the series is "good for the state", it somehow never becomes much of a point of praise when WVU wins -- which it did for the 35th time in the last 42 games.
That's small potatoes, though. Those already looking ahead to the Kansas series also missed the fact that WVU added three more home runs to its team total. That's not going to vault them up the NCAA power hitting charts but it does show that the Mountaineers have the ability to go deep.
"I think in the last probably four games, we have 20% of our home runs, something like that, right?" WVU head coach Steve Sabins questioned. (AUTH NOTE: Actually, it's 22% in the last three, which is even better.) "And so we're driving the ball and the ball starting to carry and that's what happens. They usually come in clumps and guys usually hit a little bit for more power late in their careers later in the season."
That's part of another goal -- playing more consistently down the stretch. The Mountaineers continued that trend against the Herd, which is something it needed to do in order to build that roll. It's not just going to happen, so playing crisply was vital against MU.
Again, that happened, as West Virginia was sharp in the field (no errors, one double play, one potential base stealer cut down).
"Yeah, I feel like the whole season we've been playing good ball," said Gavin Kelly, who threw out MU's Evan Bottone in the eighth in addition to cracking two home runs in his first two at-bats. "It's staying the same every day and just trying to be consistent."
Then there's the progress of starter David Hagen. While anyone checking the box score will see that he threw the five necessary innings to get the win, what they don't get is that this was a quantum progression for the Loveland, Ohio, native. He earned his fourth win of the year while throwing 62 pitches, allowing just one run on three hits and a walk, and exceeded his previous innings pitched output by two.�� If he can produce a performance like that in WVU's six remaining games, or in the postseason, the Mountaineers will have another relief arm, or a potential extra starter, upon which to build.
"In practice, his simulated game was really good," Sabins said. "And we felt like we found something and then he was able to carry that over to the game. So to be able to go five innings, that's kind of what we expect him. He's a prototypical starter."
"It definitely gives you some feel going into the next outing and some confidence that everything feels good coming out of the hand," said Hagen of his best start of the year. "Whatever role that I come into the game, it's just knowing that I gotta attack and everything's gonna be good."
Overall, the game was typical of many WVU wins this year. The Mountaineers jumped out to an early lead with the bookend pair of solo Kelly homers around a Matthew Graveline RBI single and a Matt Ineich solo shot, which reached the street outside the ballpark behind the left field wall. Marshall scratched across single runs in the fourth and seventh, but the Mountaineers responded with singletons of their own in the fifth, sixth and eighth to remain in control.
West Virginia's pitching was also effective, with Ben McDougal slotting between Hagen and Reese Bassinger, with JT Huether closing the game with a pair of strikeouts in the ninth.��
SEAMS AND BARRELS The state of GoMart Ballpark in Charleston should be an embarrassment to the city, as it certainly is not suited to host a game between the state's two Division I teams. Once again, park management did not make any indoor or covered seating available for the majority of media in attendance, placing them at a picnic table with one power strip smack in the middle of the crowd. That made for a bit of a safety hazard when it began to rain, although, fortunately, it did not come down hard enough to short anything out. Among the other shortcomings: No stat or other handouts prior to the game, a broadcast position that looked like an equipment junkyard, only a couple of reasonable photo spots, a scoreboard that suffered multiple blackouts, no setup for postgame media, with both teams doing their sessions simultaneously, and not even a complimentary bottle of water for those working the game. Reportedly (and this needs verification), this was the last season on an expiring contract to play a game here. There needs to be a serious review and more stringent standards to be followed in future deals, - -- -- -- - Politicians jumped on the chance to get their faces in front of the crowd, which was a good one if far less than the 9200 claimed by GoMart Park operators. Senator Shelley Moore Capito threw out a very creditable first pitch, while a late arriving Governor Patrick Morrisey was announced to the crowd to a healthy collection of boos. - -- -- -- - Marshall's Ian Murdoch got what appeared to be some karmaic payback in the seventh inning when smacked a home run to right after apparently doing he same thing to left. The first hit also cleared the wall, but none of the umpires on the field made a home run signal, and after a lengthy review called the hit a foul ball. Murdoch was forced to go back to the batter's box, but this time left no doubt with a high-arching fly that cleared the leaping Brock Wills at the wall. |

Once again, park management did not make any indoor or covered seating available for the majority of media in attendance, placing them at a picnic table with one power strip smack in the middle of the crowd.
